title: Kim et al. (2015): Multiple Choice
instructions: Choose the answer that best preserves the chapter's conceptual distinctions, study contexts, and limits. Read country comparisons and policy descriptions in their original historical context.

items.prompt: What central paradox introduces the chapter?
options: A visiting law immediately produced weekly in-person contact in every Chinese family
Respect for parents disappeared completely while all forms of practical support increased
Western students endorsed supporting parents as an adulthood criterion, while Asian students uniformly rejected it
Strong filial expectations can coexist with gaps in actual support and contact
items.answer: Strong filial expectations can coexist with gaps in actual support and contact
items.explanation: The chapter begins with widely endorsed obligations to respect and support parents alongside changing practices. Beliefs about what adult children should do do not necessarily describe what they actually do.

items.prompt: Which comparison between filial piety and Western filial responsibility matches the chapter?
options: Filial piety permits support only during crises and prohibits helping healthy parents
Filial responsibility requires unconditional obedience, while filial piety prioritizes independence alone
Both include support; filial piety also stresses respect, obedience, family honor, and lifelong obligation
The concepts differ only in name and assign identical meanings to receiving help
items.answer: Both include support; filial piety also stresses respect, obedience, family honor, and lifelong obligation
items.explanation: The chapter contrasts the manner, timing, and meaning of support. Its account of filial piety includes attention to parental wishes and honor and responsibility even when parents are healthy.

items.prompt: How are normative and functional solidarity distinguished?
options: Both measure the same behavior, with coresidence and respect used as interchangeable indicators
Beliefs about helping parents and actual support exchanges are separate dimensions
Stronger obligations necessarily produce more support in every family
Functional solidarity refers only to support flowing from parents to children
items.answer: Beliefs about helping parents and actual support exchanges are separate dimensions
items.explanation: Normative solidarity concerns obligations and expectations; functional solidarity concerns exchanges. Keeping them separate helps explain why strong beliefs and changing behavior can coexist.

items.prompt: What distinction does the Dual Filial Piety Model (DFPM) make?
options: Reciprocal piety emphasizes gratitude and care; authoritarian piety emphasizes hierarchy and submission
A single linear dimension explains every positive and negative consequence of filial piety
One national average captures all differences between Asian and Western filial practices
Living with parents is the only valid indicator of either type of filial piety
items.answer: Reciprocal piety emphasizes gratitude and care; authoritarian piety emphasizes hierarchy and submission
items.explanation: Reciprocal piety involves love, gratitude, and repayment of parental investment. Authoritarian piety involves compliance with parental authority and suppression of personal wishes. Both dimensions help describe continuity and change.
items.source: The two dimensions of filial piety

items.prompt: How does the chapter interpret modernization and changing filial practices?
options: Taiwan was less traditional than mainland China on every measured filial belief
Equal economic development necessarily produces identical declines in all Asian societies
Industrialization may weaken some practices, while policy and history shape different national patterns
Urbanization produced no change in any filial practice in the studies reviewed
items.answer: Industrialization may weaken some practices, while policy and history shape different national patterns
items.explanation: Some findings fit modernization accounts, but the 1990s Taiwan-China comparison complicates a uniform decline narrative. The chapter discusses different policies, institutions, and economic structures.

items.prompt: Which account best captures the possible role of government policy?
options: Family Support Agreements were entirely private promises without legal consequences or urban examples
Public and legal support can fill gaps while also changing family roles and voluntariness
Japan and South Korea had abolished their long-term care insurance programs by the chapter's publication
The authors establish that public programs fully replace families without unintended consequences
items.answer: Public and legal support can fill gaps while also changing family roles and voluntariness
items.explanation: The chapter discusses Chinese support agreements and long-term care insurance introduced in Japan in 2000 and South Korea in 2008. Possible effects on flexibility, trust, and filial support are qualifications and proposed consequences, not a universal causal verdict.
items.source: Policy and family support in the chapter's context

items.prompt: Which example illustrates a reinterpretation of filial practice?
options: Paying for high-quality residential care when direct care is unavailable
An invitation to live together cannot express filial commitment unless coresidence actually follows
Only lifelong residence in the paternal household can carry symbolic filial meaning
Professional residential care is already equally affordable and available to every Chinese family
items.answer: Paying for high-quality residential care when direct care is unavailable
items.explanation: The chapter describes costly professional care as a possible substitute for direct care when distance or schedules constrain children. It explicitly notes that such practices may be class-specific.

items.prompt: How should the chapter's cross-national coresidence percentages be interpreted?
options: The U.S. 14%, Japan 43%, and China 68.7% estimates came from one identical sampling design
High Chinese coresidence proves every arrangement begins only with parental illness and contains no conflict
Higher coresidence necessarily implies an equal proportional increase in filial beliefs and emotional closeness
They offer historical context from different studies; shared housing does not guarantee good care
items.answer: They offer historical context from different studies; shared housing does not guarantee good care
items.explanation: The estimates suggest relatively common intergenerational coresidence in the Asian settings discussed. Their sources and populations must be distinguished, and coresidence alone does not establish relationship quality or adequate support.
items.source: Comparability and meaning of coresidence rates

options: It was established as the universally best arrangement because depression was always lower than with coresidence
It requires parents and children to share one room and eliminates every form of household independence
It refers exclusively to children living abroad and providing only calls and remittances
Separate households remain nearby, without guaranteeing daily contact or better well-being
items.answer: Separate households remain nearby, without guaranteeing daily contact or better well-being
items.explanation: Nearby living can balance independence and potential support. The cited Korean comparison found more depressive symptoms among nearby, separately housed parents than among coresident parents, so proximity alone should not be assumed sufficient.

items.prompt: What helps explain intergenerational coresidence in the Asian studies reviewed?
options: Only parental illness or bereavement matters, independently of children's housing and childcare needs
Needs and resources of both generations support exchanges of housing, care, and money
Higher parental income invariably produces independent residence in every study
Traditional ideology alone determines residence, so health changes cannot precede a move
items.answer: Needs and resources of both generations support exchanges of housing, care, and money
items.explanation: Parental widowhood and health needs can prompt coresidence, while children may need housing or grandchild care. Evidence on parental economic resources is mixed, supporting attention to negotiation and mutual aid.
items.source: Needs and resources on both sides

items.prompt: Which finding illustrates support from non-coresident adult children?
options: Moving apart eliminated financial exchanges and always reduced migrants' remittances below nonmigrants'
In Korea, 57% used only remote contact while 89% reported daily face-to-face contact
Migrant children sometimes sent more money to compensate for absent hands-on care
Patrilineal norms alone explained every exchange, with no change by support type or parental side
items.answer: Migrant children sometimes sent more money to compensate for absent hands-on care
items.explanation: Living apart can constrain help with daily tasks without ending financial transfers or other contact. The chapter describes remittances as one way migration can change the form of support.

items.prompt: Why is a negative association between received support and parental well-being not sufficient evidence that help is harmful?
options: Poor health may elicit help, making parental need an alternative explanation
One cross-sectional health question removes every confounder and establishes time ordering
The same amount of help has identical effects regardless of provider or filial expectations
Harm from support is the only logically possible explanation for the association
items.answer: Poor health may elicit help, making parental need an alternative explanation
items.explanation: Parents with poorer health may receive more help, so cross-sectional studies can mix causes of support with consequences of support. Cultural expectations and the source of help may also matter.

items.prompt: How can the meaning of support depend on cultural expectations?
options: Only the quantity matters; provider identity and beliefs have no role
Provider expectations, familism, and filial beliefs can shape support's meaning and associations
Help from daughters-in-law always reduces depression by the same amount throughout Asia
Stronger filial beliefs necessarily increase every caregiver's burden
items.answer: Provider expectations, familism, and filial beliefs can shape support's meaning and associations
items.explanation: The chapter reviews links involving culturally expected providers, parents' familism, and children's filial beliefs. These may qualify the associations of receiving or providing support with well-being and burden.

items.prompt: Which approach would better capture emotional closeness in the families discussed?
options: Assess indirect expressions and relationship quality alongside concerns about harmony and face
Count explicit requests alone and interpret fewer requests as proof that family ties are unimportant
Treat cross-national differences in naming close kin as direct measures of objective relationship quality
Measure only instrumental assistance and ignore emotional ties or generational differences in appraisal
items.answer: Assess indirect expressions and relationship quality alongside concerns about harmony and face
items.explanation: People may avoid explicit requests because they worry about burdening others, disrupting harmony, or losing face. The chapter therefore calls for culturally sensitive measures rather than equating less overt expression with weak relationships.

items.prompt: Which account best captures the two levels of intergenerational ambivalence?
options: Ambivalence means indifference, with neither positive nor negative feelings about a relationship
It arises solely from indecisive personality and has no connection to paid work or caregiving roles
Contradictory social roles and mixed feelings about the same relationship are distinct but related levels
The rural Chinese evidence shows severe conflict in every parent-child relationship
items.answer: Contradictory social roles and mixed feelings about the same relationship are distinct but related levels
items.explanation: Structural or sociological ambivalence concerns competing role demands; subjective or psychological ambivalence concerns simultaneous positive and negative sentiments. The chapter identifies these as promising but understudied perspectives in Asian family research.
